articles.title: UAAP suspends Ateneo coach Louie Alas for one game
articles.summary: Just days after losing to rival La Salle, the Ateneo Blue Eagles look to rebound against the FEU Tamaraws minus head coach Louie Alas

blocks.text: MENTOR. Ateneo coach Louie Alas (left) instructs his players on court.
UAAP
Just days after losing to rival La Salle, the Ateneo Blue Eagles look to rebound against the FEU Tamaraws minus head coach Louie Alas
MANILA, Philippines – The UAAP suspended Ateneo head coach Louie Alas on Friday, October 9, after accumulating three infractions in the men’s basketball tournament.
Alas will serve a one-game suspension on Saturday, October 10, when the Blue Eagles battle the Far Eastern University Tamaraws at the Araneta Coliseum.
Ateneo, fresh from a loss to rival La Salle, remains locked in a three-way tie for second at 3-2, behind FEU (3-1) early in the first round of Season 89.

Alas committed two of his three infractions during Ateneo’s game against the La Salle Green Archers on Wednesday, October 7, while his first technical foul came on September 19, during the Blue Eagles’ match against the UP Fighting Maroons.
League rules state that coaches will be slapped an automatic one-game suspension after accumulating three technical fouls or infractions.

During the Ateneo-La Salle game, Blue Eagles assistant coach Kerby Raymundo was observed verbally taunting La Salle player Vhoris Marasigan from the bench following a foul call at the 3:42 mark of the fourth quarter. Alas was subsequently assessed a direct technical foul for unsportsmanlike behavior, which was later changed to a bench technical foul.

Around the same time, Alas was observed engaging in physical misconduct when he forcefully attempted to pull a La Salle player to his feet before making further physical contact by nudging another player with his elbow.

The actions were not seen by game officials, but the Commissioner’s Office reviewed the incidents and assessed the physical misconduct as a disqualifying foul under the UAAP House Rules and applicable FIBA regulations.
During the Ateneo-UP game, Raymundo was assessed a technical foul for improper bench decorum, which was charged to Alas.
Ateneo can appeal the decision. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Bosnia and Herzegovina will soon have a new Grand Mufti
articles.summary: The new leader of the Islamic Community in Bosnia and Herzegovina will be elected on October 10. The reis-ul-ulema's role is not only important for Muslims in the country itself, but could inspire…

image.caption: The headquarters of the Islamic Community of Bosnia and Herzegovina are in SarajevoImage: Samir Huseinović/DW

blocks.text: The reis-ul-ulema or Grand Mufti of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the head of the country's Islamic community, represents the interests of Muslims before the state, expresses himself on political, moral and social issues and defends the independence of the Islamic Community in Bosnia and Herzegovina against attempts at foreign influence.
Having served two seven-year terms, the current Grand Mufti, Husein Kavazovic, is no longer permitted to run.

Three candidates are competing to become his successor: Salem Dedovic, the Mufti of Mostar, Nedzad Grabus, the Mufti of Sarajevo, and Mensur Malkic, the head of the Directorate for Religious Affairs of the Islamic Community in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Grand Mufti's envoy.

While Malkic's focus lies in strengthening the Islamic Community in religious and institutional terms, Dedovic has stated that he sees the office in a more political light and would like it to become more engaged in social debates. Grabus, who has the most international experience as the former Grand Mufti of Slovenia, says he would like to strengthen the community in times of globalization and secularization.

"No other Islamic personality in Europe holds a position like the Reis-ul-ulema in Sarajevo," said Imam Benjamin Idriz, the head of the Islamic Community in the Bavarian city of Penzberg and the chair of the Munich Forum for Islam. "That's why the importance of this election extends far beyond the country, to Muslims and non-Muslims alike, across Europe."

blocks.caption: Grand Mufti Husein Kavazovic has reached the end of his two termsImage: Samir Jordamovic/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: The President of the Islamic Community of Bosniaks in Germany (IGBD), Zenahir Mrakovic, said that the "election is important to us, because historically, theologically and institutionally, we share close ties with the Islamic Community of Bosnia and Herzegovina."
"Bosniak" is the name Bosnian Muslims use for themselves. With around 100 communities across the country, the IGBD is one of Germany's smaller Muslim associations.

Muslims have lived in Bosnia and Herzegovina for centuries. Islam was introduced to the population when to Ottoman Empire spread through southeastern Europe. The organizational structure of the Islamic Communities was established after the Berlin Congress in 1878, which, among other things, placed Bosnia and Herzegovina under Austro-Hungarian rule.

Following the example of Christian churches, the Austro-Hungarian rulers soon officially recognized Islam as a religious community and in 1882, they founded the Council of Ulema and appointed the first Reis-ul-ulema as president.
Unique self-organization of the Muslim faith

This kind of Islamic self-organization could become a model for Muslims across Europe. The Islamic Community of Bosnia and Herzegovina is independent from the state and is financed with donations, membership fees and zakat, a form of charity given by Muslims.

The Islamic Community has its own sort of parliament, the Sabor, and a Constitutional Court that ensures the community's actions are in line with the constitution of the country in which it operates. The Riyaset is the community's highest executive body, responsible for implementing decisions. Its headquarters are in Sarajevo.

In the 150 years since its founding, the Islamic Community of Bosnia and Herzegovina has survived numerous political upheavals and repeatedly adapted to new circumstances. After the Ottoman Empire came the Habsburg monarchy and Austro-Hungarian rule, then the Kingdom of Yugoslavia and the Republic of Yugoslavia under Josip Broz Tito. Following Tito's death, the Bosnian War for independence ended in 1995 with the Dayton Accords.

Today, Bosnia and Herzegovina is a secular state with a democratic constitutional order. Time and again, the Islamic Community has clearly distanced itself from radical tendencies. It has a history of cooperation and coexistence with Jewish and Christian communities.
This has also left an impression on the roughly 400,000 Bosnian Muslims living in Germany.

"In the process of institutionalizing Islam in Germany, the experience of the Bosniaks' Islamic Community should be taken more strongly into account," said Esnaf Begic, a former imam and a lecturer at the Institute for Islamic Theology at Osnabrück University. "We are autochthonous European Muslims and to a certain extent, we share more similarities with Germans than with Muslims from Afghanistan, Iran or Saudi Arabia."

Mrakovic, head of the IGBD, agrees that Bosnia's experience with organizing religious life in a democratic and pluralistic society could also be useful to other Muslim communities. "It's not about telling other people how to live their Islamic faith but about learning from our own experiences: how we preserve our religious identity while remaining a natural part of European, democratic society.

blocks.caption: Islamic feminism is more widespread in Bosnia and HerzegovinaImage: Samir Huseinović/DW

blocks.text: An office in challenging times

The new head of Bosnian Muslims will be assuming his role in challenging times. Statehood in Bosnia and Herzegovina remains fragile, and foreign actors are vying for more influence. "Attempts to exert more influence aren't only coming from Ankara or Riyah, but also from Washington, Berlin or Brussels. They, too are, trying to act upon the Reis-ul-ulema in their own interest," Begic said.

In Europe, anti-Muslim racism and Islamophobia have reached levels that are becoming increasingly frightening for Muslims. Right-wing populists are on the rise, and extremist parties are attracting more and more supporters bent on denying Muslims the right to participate in society.
Given the circumstances, the new Reis-ul-ulema will be expected to employ the full democratic and historical legitimacy of his office to actively engage in debates about Islam in Europe.

This is what Idriz, the imam from Penzberg, hopes for, too. He believes the new Reis-ul-ulema could inspire more confidence not only in Bosniaks, but in all European Muslims, while signaling to majority societies that Islam is a part of Europe, and that it affirms and embraces values such as the rule of law, gender equality and freedom of expression. "In the future, the Reis-ul-ulema should lay an even stronger emphasis on this," Idriz said.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Finland: The world's happiest country has a debt problem it can no longer ignore
articles.summary: Finns have many reasons to feel content, but the country's debt pile is not one of them. Russia's war in Ukraine has added to the fiscal burden. So can the Nordic nation absorb another shock?

image.caption: Finland's policymakers will spend the winter deciding where the ax should fallImage: Ardan Fuessmann/IMAGO

blocks.text: There's an uneasy mood in Finland — the country ranked the world's happiest for nine consecutive years . A colder-than-usual winter is on the way and so is the toughest austerity budget in years.
With an election due in April, the argument is no longer how much to cut, but which services, benefits and pensions will face the biggest cuts.

Finland's debt and deficit levels are in their worst state since the 1990s, when a banking crash and the collapse of the Soviet Union — a key export partner — pushed the Nordic nation into its own Great Depression.
Finland's debt ratio climbed sharply since COVID
Last month, Statistics Finland confirmed that the national debt had reached 90.3% of gross domestic product (GDP) in the second quarter. Before the pandemic, that figure was about 65%.

Trouble to the east is, again, part of the reason. Finland ramped up defense spending after joining NATO a year afterRussia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Helsinki, which used to rely on Moscow for about a third of its energy, also faced much higher costs as it transitioned to other suppliers.

Yet, the Finnish government has spent more than it earns since the 2008/9 Global Financial Crisis, partly due to an aging population and sluggish economic growth. Last month, the State Treasury projected the fiscal deficit would reach 4.2% of GDP in 2026.
EU scrutiny over growing deficit

Brussels has piled pressure on Helsinki to bring down the borrowing gap, as European Union rules require member states to stay below 3% of GDP. In January, the European Council opened an excessive deficit procedure and gave Finland until the end of 2028 to reach the desired target.

Prime Minister Petteri Orpo’s government, which took office in June 2023, said it would aim to save about €9 billion during this parliamentary term. But whoever wins the next election will have to cut much deeper, economists warn.
"The amounts currently estimated range from €8 to €11 billion," Jarkko Kivisto, an advisor to the Bank of Finland's Monetary Policy and Research Department, told DW.
Earlier this year, all but one political party agreed to support a debt brake, where the next government commits to tightening the country's deficit to 2-2.5% of GDP by 2031.
Finland: Europe's race for critical raw materials
PM says 'no' to tax hikes

Orpo's center-right National Coalition is the only party to date to promise a further €9 billion in cuts, if he wins a second term. As well as further savings from health, social care and welfare, Orpo also plans to target workplace pensions, without reducing current payouts.
While the Social Democrats plan to split the reforms between spending cuts and tax hikes, Orpo plans to achieve his target without raising taxes, meaning public services will bear the brunt.
Kivisto, however, cautioned: "The deficit is so large that it would need a package that includes tax increases and expenditure cuts."

While Finland's at-risk-of-poverty rate is lower than the EU average, unemployment is higher than anywhere else in the bloc. In August, Finland's jobless total stood at 10.3%, just above Spain's 10%, according to Eurostat, the bloc's statistics agency. Youth unemployment reached 23.3%, against an EU average of 15.4%.
With household spending already falling, Lauri Olappa, director of the Finnish Centre for New Economic Analysis, warned that a new round of austerity would be a hard blow for the domestic economy.

"More than a quarter of the population works in the public sector, so if those workers face the threat of being sacked, the savings rate will rise and private spending will drop again," Olappa told DW.

Successive pressures ranging from COVID, higher interest rates and the impact of two wars have hurt efforts to cut the growing gap between income and borrowing. The 2027 budget proposal still counts on a spending gap of €12.4 billion.

blocks.caption: Finland hiked defense spending, including an order for F-35 jets, due to the threat from RussiaImage: Jeremy Lock/REUTERS

blocks.text: Finland re-arms after Russia’s full-scale invasion
Before the Ukraine war, Finland had already committed to buying 64 F-35A fighter jets from the United States, in a deal worth about €8.4 billion.

During more than four years of Russia's war in Ukraine, the Nordic nation raised military spending from $4.5 billion to over $8 billion per year, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI).
In April, the government said it would further hike defense spending to 3.2% of GDP, close to NATO's 3.5% target.
A night in Finland's largest underground defense bunker

With oil prices remaining close to $100 a barrel due to the Iran war, the government has so far resisted pressure to increase fuel subsidies. That's despite the Bank of Finland recording a 50% rise in the cost of imported energy in the early months of the Iran war.

While Finland’s shift to renewables, along with the opening of the Olkiluoto 3 nuclear reactor in 2023, has cushioned a worse energy crisis, the central bank warned this summer that sustained high oil and gas prices would mean "lower economic growth and higher inflation" next year.

On another positive note, parts of Finland's export sector are booming, thanks to strong metal and shipbuilding orders, which Olappa described as strong as "the boom years of Nokia," when the once market-leading phone maker carried Finnish economic growth.
"There is a possibility that the export sector can steer us out of this recession," he told DW, as long as demand from the rest of Europe remains strong.

blocks.caption: Despite their money woes, Finns are consistently ranked as the world’s happiest peopleImage: Depositphotos/IMAGO

blocks.text: Markets give Helsinki time to reform

Despite the multiple roadblocks to bringing down the deficit, market reaction to Finland's debt woes has, so far, been muted. Rating agencies have kept the country's outlook stable, apart from S&P, which turned negative in April without cutting the rating.

On October 6, the premium the Finnish government pays over Germany to borrow for 10 years was 38 basis points. That compares to 128 for France and 107 for Italy. In other words, investors still treat Finnish debt as among the safest in Europe.
That is, as long as the next shock is not a longer oil-price spike, a fresh escalation from Russia, or a euro-area debt crisis centered on France.

Next March, Finland could yet be named the planet’s happiest nation for a 10th year in a row. How long the smiles last, once the bill for decades of borrowing arrives a month later, is anyone’s guess.

articles.title: OpenAI projected to bring in $20bn less in revenue than expected
articles.summary:
Questions raised over AI growth as ChatGPT maker forecasts this year’s revenue at $50bn, way below the $70bn signalled before

OpenAI has revealed that it is making about $20bn less in…

blocks.text: OpenAI has revealed that it is making about $20bn less in projected revenue than it had recently indicated to investors, raising questions about the break-neck growth rate in demand for AI.
The ChatGPT-maker company has told investors that its revenues for this year would reach $50bn (£37bn), a projection based on sales up to the end of September.
However, this is significantly less than the $70bn that it had signalled in information provided to investors last month, which was widely reported.

Forecasts of annualised revenues by the leading artificial intelligence players, including by OpenAI’s rival Anthropic, the maker of Claude, are closely watched by markets as an indicator of overall demand for a technology that is attracting huge investment.
OpenAI is in early-stage talks to raise $30bn in a funding round that values the business at about $1.4tn.
News of the $20bn gap buffeted US tech stocks on Thursday, with the tech-led Nasdaq closing down by 1.4%. Chip giant Nvidia fell 2.9%, Oracle was down 5.5% and Micron declined 4.8%.

The discrepancy arose from attempts by OpenAI investors to provide a more direct comparison with how projected revenue is measured by Anthropic, which hit $65bn in forecast revenue by the end of July.
Anthropic includes the revenue from sales via cloud partners, such as Amazon’s AWS and Google Cloud, while OpenAI does not.
Last month, Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, said that the company would not float on the stock market this year as had been expected, citing safety concerns over AI.
Altman’s decision followed cases of AI agents going rogue to hack external systems and AI ​safety researchers quitting their companies concerned about the technology’s risks.

Democrat and Republican politicians are calling for new rules to govern AI systems, after two researchers from Anthropic warned that the lightning pace of development of AI without safeguards could lead to the extinction of the human race.
after newsletter promotion
Anthropic is expected to push ahead with plans for an initial public offering (IPO) as soon as next month.
OpenAI’s most recent fundraising was in March when it closed a $122bn round of finance at a valuation of $852bn.
Two months later Anthropic announced it had raised $65bn, valuing the company at $965bn.

articles.title: How good is this year's flu shot? Here's what to know about flu season
articles.summary: Health officials say flu season has arrived early this year, but how worried should Canadians be? As we head into Thanksgiving weekend, the CBC looks at where the flu is hitting hardest and how you…

image.caption: As we head into cold and flu season, some experts are expecting less severe illness due to a milder strain of flu dominating so far, but the early start to the flu season has others stressing early prevention methods. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

blocks.text: Walking down the street this week, it may seem like everyone is sneezing and hacking up a lung. But as health officials announce the start of an earlier than usual flu season, how worried should Canadians be? And as we head into Thanksgiving weekend, should we be scrambling to update flu and COVID-19 shots?

Some experts say that while this year's flu season may have arrived on our doorstep sooner than usual, it's not necessarily a cause for alarm — but other experts are stressing the importance of prevention in heavy-hit regions such as Toronto and Calgary, where authorities reported one person had already died from the virus.

The strain making up roughly 98 per cent of cases in Canada so far tends to be a milder one, according to Brian Ward, professor emeritus at the Research Institute of the McGill University Health Centre in Montreal.

"So far at least, this looks like an H1N1 dominated year, and the years where H1N1 dominates, you can have very large outbreaks, but the number or the proportion of people … who get very sick, is relatively small compared to years that are dominated by H3N2," he told CBC News.
"I'm not convinced yet that we're actually seeing the beginning of a real outbreak. What we're seeing is sort of isolated, small outbreaks."
But where the flu is striking, doctors say it's striking hard. There are currently more than 400 confirmed flu cases in Alberta, where vaccines aren't yet widely available.

items: Doctors say flu season is ahead of schedule this year as cases pop up across Ontario
1 dead, more than 400 confirmed flu cases ahead of vaccine availability in Alberta

blocks.text: Some regions have started rolling out flu and COVID-19 shots to high-risk populations, with most regions set to offer shots to the general public by mid-October.
Here's what we know.
Is everyone getting sick right now?
According to the latest national numbers, which include data on influenza trends up to Sept. 26, there have been 2,102 detections of influenza across the country since the end of August.

It's an early start to the season. Between Sept. 20 and Sept. 26, 3.7 per cent of influenza tests came back positive, much higher than the average 0.5 per cent rate seen this time of year in 2023-2025.

items: Nova Scotia opens COVID-19, flu vaccine bookings ahead of respiratory illness season
Flu and COVID-19 vaccinations underway in B.C. as respiratory illness season arrives early
Vaccine-preventable illnesses on the horizon again as Canadian kids head back to school

blocks.text: But much of this national increase is driven by an uptick of cases in B.C. and Yukon, and in large cities such as Toronto and Calgary. The person who died in Alberta lived in the Calgary area and was in the 70-79 years age range, authorities say.
"The rest of the country is really very quiet," Ward said.
B.C. warns of early start to flu season, launches fall immunization campaign
He noted that in B.C., outbreaks in long-term care homes are driving the increase in cases, warning that families getting together this holiday weekend could result in further spread.
"That may be the seed that moves the virus … into the schools and universities and marketplaces and so on. But overall, we're still below the 5 per cent [epidemic] threshold."
Official figures don't catch every case of flu, as not everyone seeks out a test when they fall ill.

In hard-hit Toronto, family doctor Joseph Param told CBC News the increase of flu patients he's seeing at his practice is mainly among young adults who are more likely to travel on public transit and may still go to work when feeling under the weather, perhaps because they're used to flu season starting later.
You're not imagining it — flu season has started early this year
"Over the last couple of weeks, patients who are very healthy who see me rarely have been coming in with severe symptoms," he said.
"So it is important that the general population is aware that we are seeing … early cases now and so that we start taking precautions earlier than expected."
Doctors advise Canadians to stay home if they feel ill and to get vaccinated as soon as shots become available in their area, particularly with the long weekend coming up.
How effective is the flu shot this year?
The protection of flu shots varies from year to year depending on the most dominant strain of influenza in your area.

This year, it's a "good" match, Ward said. Although H3N2 viruses dominated for much of 2025, that subtype hasn't cropped up much in 2026, and this year's vaccine is well-positioned to protect against H1N1.
He said "influenza viruses march to their own drummers" and can mutate even within one flu season.

It's not just flu season in Canada — historically, we see more respiratory illnesses in general cropping up during the fall and going into winter, including colds and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), the latter of which is most dangerous in young children.
Around 98 per cent of lab-confirmed cases of influenza in Canada since the end of August have been of the H1N1 strain, according to government data. (New Africa/Shutterstock)

Rates of COVID-19 are currently trending lower right now than last year, with 3.8 per cent of tests coming back positive in the last week of September compared with 10.3 per cent at the same time in 2025.

The National Advisory Committee on Immunizations (NACI) said in September that it continues to "strongly recommend" the latest COVID-19 booster shots for those at a higher risk of developing severe COVID-19, including health-care workers, adults over the age of 65, those with immunocompromised systems and people in long-term care homes.
When can I get my flu and COVID-19 shots?

Several provinces such as Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia are already advising residents that appointments for flu vaccines and COVID-19 booster shots are available now for residents over the age of six months.
New Brunswick, Saskatchewan and Manitoba are currently allowing residents to book their flu and COVID-19 vaccines, with immunization efforts officially kicking off on Oct. 13.
Those living in Newfoundland and Labrador can receive flu and COVID-19 shots starting Oct. 19.
In Ontario, flu and COVID-19 immunizations have been available since last week for high-risk groups, but don't open to the general public until Oct. 26.

In Quebec, you can start making appointments as of Oct. 13, but the flu and COVID-19 vaccination campaign itself doesn't begin until Oct. 20. It is only free to eligible residents deemed high-risk, meaning non-eligible residents must pay for the shots.

items: Updated COVID-19, flu vaccines available in N.B. on Oct. 13
Alberta now providing free RSV antibodies to newborns after calls from pediatricians to expand access

blocks.text: Flu and COVID-19 shots can be booked now in Alberta, with the first appointments starting Oct. 19. While flu shots are free to everyone, Albertans who aren't considered high-risk for COVID-19 will have to pay.
In B.C., those registered in their Get Vaccinated system will receive a notification reminding them to get their flu shots. Flu and COVID-19 shots are available starting Oct. 13.

COVID-19 and flu shots will be available at specific clinics in the Northwest Territories this fall, but a timeline hasn't been released yet. Those in Yukon have been able to book appointments for flu and COVID-19 shots since the end of September. No details have been released for Nunavut's rollout as of Oct. 8.
Before heading out to the pharmacy, it's important to check the requirements in your area to be sure that you're eligible. Most regions offer RSV vaccines to eligible patients as well.

In the future, we could see more variety in our flu vaccines: an mRNA influenza vaccine made by Moderna was approved by the FDA in the U.S. in the summer, making this the first flu season it'll face. It's still under review by Health Canada.

articles.title: The Social Reckoning is not only not as good as The Social Network, it's also not good enough to hate
articles.summary: Though Aaron Sorkin's The Social Reckoning positions itself as endlessly relevant, it's so vapid and made with such disinterest that it resists serious hatred. The follow-up to 2010's…

image.caption: Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in a scene from The Social Reckoning. (Leah Gallo/Sony Pictures/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Entertainment·REVIEW

Though Aaron Sorkin's The Social Reckoning positions itself as endlessly relevant, it's so vapid and made with such disinterest that it resists serious hatred. The follow-up to 2010's Facebook-takedown The Social Network is an insulting bore with very little insight or opinion to disagree with, let alone productively hate.
Aaron Sorkin's follow-up to Facebook-takedown The Social Network is an almost astounding letdown
Hating a movie can be just as productive, and potentially more entertaining, than loving it.

A film that's egregiously stupid, poorly thought-out or just plain evil can provide just as much fodder for thought and discussion as one that's genuinely moving. In both cases, there's at least something to care about.

Which is what makes it so disappointing to encounter something like The Social Reckoning. Because the Aaron Sorkin written-and-directed sequel to The Social Network — 2010's incredible Facebook origin story written by Sorkin and directed by David Fincher — is one of those rare, deplorable anti-art creations.

One of those movies that's so vapid and unoriginal it resists serious hatred, even while trying to position itself as endlessly relevant. In general, it's such an insulting bore that it lacks enough insight or opinion to even disagree with, let alone productively hate.

Which, being about the scourge of social media and corporate controlled groupthink, could make it an example of the problem Sorkin attempts to expose: there's no shortage of low-quality, uninteresting "content" clogging our feeds and For You pages.
But this fumbling of fertile source material comes courtesy of a cast and crew that features some of the more interesting creatives currently working.

The Social Reckoning charts Facebook's period of endless growth and promises to be a take-down of one of the three tech oligarchs of the apocalypse. (The other two being depicted in Alex Gibney's documentary Musk, slated for an Oct. 16 release in Canada, and Luca Guadagnino's Sam Altman/OpenAI critique Artificial that just premiered to rave reviews at the New York Film Festival.)

The implicit sales pitch here is that this is an incisive and timely piece that will open eyes and turn the world on its head. But instead of Spotlight, here's what we get: The Bear's Jeremy Allen White plays Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz, a reporter at a struggling (what's new?) outlet trying to retain readers flocking to social media. And Anora's Mikey Madison plays Frances Haugen, a disillusioned product manager working for Facebook's civic misinformation team.

To the surprise of absolutely no one, they quickly find one another and begin to unravel and expose a secretive pattern of malpractice going by the name of MSI (Meaningful Social Interactions) that has come to destabilize governments, rot brains and destroy the very nature of truth. Again, what else is new?
Meanwhile, Succession's Jeremy Strong plays big-bad Mark Zuckerberg on a precipitous fall from grace, both in terms of the character's in-universe PR and in terms of how he's been portrayed on film.
Here, Zuckerberg is staring down studio lights, prepping for a hearing on his company's contribution to the destruction of liberal democracy and the mental health of children around the globe.

Compared to Jesse Eisenberg's layered, barbed and infinitely fascinating interpretation, which earned him his first and only acting Oscar nomination, this Zuckerberg comes off as more uninspired and poorly thought out than the Metaverse he created.

If it weren't for the carnival-esque way Strong brings out the infamously alien characteristics of a man once forced to publicly claim he was not actually a lizard, he'd be almost entirely incidental to the plot.
Mikey Madison, left, and Jeremy Allen White star in The Social Reckoning. (Leah Gallo/Sony Pictures/The Associated Press)

Outside the terrifyingly controlled mannerisms of a socially awkward praying mantis — and a haircut somewhere between Fargo's Ole Munch and Starburst's Berries and Cream man — this Zuckerberg stays firmly in the background.

Zuckerberg's motivations drove the singular and direct original, making it a compelling psychoanalytical character study. This time, we get almost nothing narratively from the man who instead peers oddly from corners and mostly unimportant side scenes, unsettling you with the occasional reminder that he exists, before once again proving that, in the grand scheme of things, he doesn't actually have much influence over how any of this plays out.
That is, so far as this mundane, unilaterally boring and unimaginably cliché narrative is concerned.

Sorkin's Zuckerberg operates like a cheap marketing gimmick, set dressing to trick audiences into watching the exasperated but enamoured reporter Horwitz guide the headstrong, heart-of-gold Haugen into battle with the all-powerful man behind the curtain. Like an amateur screenwriter's version of The Client, but with more computers.

This is not entirely Strong's fault. From his endlessly pathetic and committed turn as Kendall Roy, to his scene-stealing performance as Trump's fixer Roy Cohn in The Apprentice, we know that if there was any narrative meat on the bones to chew here, he undoubtedly would have found it.

Instead, the blame can be laid squarely at the feet of Sorkin. For those who already can't stand the West Wing and Moneyball writer's racing, stylized dialogue and stilted circumstances, this will perhaps come as no surprise. But even for those who love the heightened reality schtick of the Sorkinverse, The Social Reckoning is nothing but a disappointment.

items: Jacob Tremblay can relate to the Unabomber. No, really
Tom Cruise is fantastic in Digger. You might hate it

blocks.text: Here, all we get is a hamfisted and saccharine story that somehow both exploits and glosses over its topical and prescient issues. A meandering, self-indulgent collage of journalism tropes that leads to White and Madison directly referencing other, better journalism movies in their on-screen dialogue.
And it all culminates in an ending so incredibly, unbelievably trite it almost makes you think Sorkin was actively trying to send up the sentimental text-on-screen ending of Stand By Me.

But the worst thing about The Social Reckoning is not any of this. It's everything between these failings. It is the almost total and absolute lack of risk, specificity or intent. It is the fact that the movie's entire runtime seems to operate as an excuse to take up time. It's the fact that Sorkin — an Academy and Emmy-award winning writer — has crafted something so completely neutered that it barely merits hatred.

This is bad for comparative purposes: While The Social Network used the founding of Facebook as a scaffold to investigate its creator's psyche, Reckoning uses it as set dressing to illustrate a Wikipedia entry that isn't even particularly accurate.

But beyond comparisons to its predecessor, Reckoning is also disappointing because it lacks anything to dislike. It is disappointing for its general greyness and its cowardice. And that, more than anything else, is the worst thing a piece of art can be.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jackson Weaver is a reporter and film critic for CBC's entertainment news team in Toronto. You can reach him at jackson.weaver@cbc.ca.

blocks.text: Published October 9, 2026 3:48pm

Senator-judge Risa Hontiveros on Friday claimed that a Ukrainian company that remitted funds to Cale88 Foods Corporation, one of the listed business interests of Vice President Sara Duterte’s husband, Manases Carpio, was possibly involved in money laundering.
Hontiveros raised this during her interjection on Day 37 of the trial, where Article 2 of the impeachment case is being tackled, accusing the Vice President of amassing unexplained wealth.
The senator-judge said that her office reviewed the other foreign-based companies that sent funds to Cale88, aside from those based in China.

“Lumalabas na at least isa doon, ay posibleng sangkot sa money laundering activities. Dito po sa country, Ukraine, the Cale88 list of foreign transactions identifies a Ukrainian remitter by the name of Arkmen LLC using registration number 41423974. The address stated in the list is Zoriana 30A, Tsybuliv, Ukraine,” Hontiveros said.

(It appears that at least one of them is possibly involved in money laundering activities. The Cale88 listed foreign transactions from Ukraine, identifying a Ukrainian remitter by the name of Arkmen LLC using registration number 41423974. The address stated in the list is Zoriana 30A, Tsybuliv, Ukraine.)

“At itong registration number, 41423974, at ‘yung address Zoriana 30A, ay nagko-correspond sa isang kumpanya involved sa isang criminal proceeding na binuksan po nung May 19, 2025 para sa fraud and money laundering kaugnay ng 1.225 million euros,” she added.

(The registration number and the address Zoriana 30A correspond to a company involved in a criminal proceeding initiated on May 19, 2025, for fraud and money laundering involving 1.225 million euros.)
Hontiveros said that in March 2026, the Pecherskyi District Court of Kyiv ordered a search of Arkmen’s premises, and in April 2026, it ordered a freeze on the suspect's 100% shareholding in Arkmen.
“At ‘yung huling inward remittance po nitong Arkmen LLC sa Cale88 ay noong May 30, 2025 na pagkatapos na po ng petsa ng pagsisimula ng criminal proceedings,” she said.
(The last inward remittance from Arkmen LLC to Cale88 was on May 30, 2025—which was shortly after the criminal proceedings began.)

The senator-judge thus asked prosecution witness, Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) Office of the Commissioner chief of staff Atty. Anne Loraine Garcia-Marquez, if there were legitimate transactions behind the international remittances between Arkmen LLC and Cale88, Carpio’s firm should have reported them as sales and subjected them to tax.
Garcia-Marquez answered, “Kung ito po ay sales po, then it should have been reported po in the annual Income Tax Return po.”
(If these are sales, then it should have been reported in the annual Income Tax Return.)

To recall, Hontiveros previously claimed that some of the Chinese firms that funded Cale88 were state-owned enterprises that may be “advancing the interests of the Chinese Communist Party.” —AOL, GMA News

blocks.text: One hour to go
It’s one hour to go until we learn who is the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize winner.
10am UK, 11am CEST.

blocks.caption: The room where a press conference will be given to announce the winner of the Nobel Peace Prize 2026 at the Nobel Institute in Oslo, Norway. Photograph: Javad Parsa/NTB/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Last year’s peace prize was won by Venezuelan politician María Corina Machado for her dogged struggle to rescue the South American country from its fate as “a brutal, authoritarian state”.
She later presented her award to Donald Trump, meeting him in the White House, nearly a fortnight after he ordered the abduction of Venezuela’s president, Nicolás Maduro.
In his 1895 will, Swedish chemist and inventor Alfred Nobel wrote:

“All of my remaining realisable assets are to be disbursed as follows: the capital, converted to safe securities by my executors, is to constitute a fund, the interest on which is to be distributed annually as prizes to those who, during the preceding year, have conferred the greatest benefit to humankind. The interest is to be divided into five equal parts and distributed as follows: one part to the person who made the most important discovery or invention in the field of physics; one part to the person who made the most important chemical discovery or improvement; one part to the person who made the most important discovery within the domain of physiology or medicine; one part to the person who, in the field of literature, produced the most outstanding work in an ideal direction; and one part to the person who has done the most or best to advance fellowship among nations, the abolition or reduction of standing armies, and the establishment and promotion of peace congresses. The prizes for physics and chemistry are to be awarded by the Swedish Academy of Sciences; that for physiological or medical achievements by the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm; that for literature by the Academy in Stockholm; and that for champions of peace by a committee of five persons to be selected by the Norwegian Storting. It is my express wish that when awarding the prizes, no consideration be given to nationality, but that the prize be awarded to the worthiest person, whether or not they are Scandinavian.”
And here we are, 125 years later!
The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor, which is about €1.1m or £910,000.
Morning opening: Who will win the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize?

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa
The 2026 Nobel Peace Prize will be announced this morning, with all sorts of speculation about who could be this year’s worthy winner.
(Despite his hopes, Donald Trump is very unlikely to win it, again.)
Mykola Kuleba and Save Ukraine who work on rescuing Ukrainian children abducted by Russia during the war have long been among the favourites, alongside Sudan’s Emergency Response Rooms.

But in the last few hours, Yulia Navalnaya, the wife of late Alexei Navalny, has gone straight to the very top of the list on some popular prediction websites. Could she be the one – just days after Vladimir Putin’s birthday in Russia?
Well: no one really knows, except a handful of members of the Norwegian Nobel Committee.
Its chair Jørgen Watne Frydnes will appear in front of cameras at 10am UK time (11am CEST) this morning to give us the name of the winner.
We will bring it live to you here.
It’s Friday, 9 October 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.

articles.title: Palace denies hand in Mark Villar's move to majority, hits Alan Cayetano
articles.summary: Malacañang on Friday rejected Senator Alan Peter Cayetano's claim that the Marcos administration played a role in Senator Mark Villar's recent transfer to the majority.
articles.byline: LYJAH TIFFANY BONZO, JONATHAN ANDAL, GMA News

blocks.text: Published October 9, 2026 3:31pm
Malacañang on Friday rejected Senator Alan Peter Cayetano's claim that the Marcos administration played a role in Senator Mark Villar's recent transfer to the majority.
In a press briefing on Friday, Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro said duly-elected senators think independently and cannot be forced to act against their will.

"May mga sariling isipan at pagdedesisyon ang mga senador. Hindi sila maaaring diktahan, dahil kung sila ay madidiktahan at wala silang pag-iisip, hindi sila dapat na binoboto ng taong-bayan," Castro said.

(Senators have their own minds, they can make their own decisions. They cannot be dictated upon, because if this were so and the lack independent thought, the public shouldn't vote for them in the first place.)
Reacting to Villar's transfer to the majority on Thursday, Cayetano wished the senator well and noted that he understands "too well the circumstances that lead to changes in political alliances."
Cayetano said that since May, it has become "increasingly clear how important it is for this administration to maintain a closely allied working majority in the Senate."

"But regardless of how the political landscape shifts, our duty remains unchanged. We will continue to stand for what is right, uphold our institutions, and work for the good of our nation," he added.
Castro asked Cayetano if he was thinking this way because he had experienced something similar during the previous administration.

"So 'yan lang dapat natin iparating kay Senator Alan Cayetano, dahil kung ganito ang kaniyang iniisip, naranasan niya ba ito sa panahon ng dating Pangulong Duterte, na ang kanilang mga miyembro sa Senado ay nadidiktahan?" she added.

(So that is what we should convey to Senator Alan Cayetano, because if this is how he thinks, did he experience this during former President Duterte's time—that members of the Senate were being dictated upon?)
The Senate majority now stands at 14 members following Villar's move.
Not guaranteed
According to Castro, Villar's jump to the Senate majority does not mean that he is no longer an ally of Vice President Sara Duterte, who is facing an impeachment trial.
She noted that this also cannot determine or predict where the impeachment trial is headed now.

"So kahit maging miyembro ang karamihan sa kanila or rather ang iba sa kanila sa majority, hindi naman nangangahulugan na magdidikta sila kung ano ang mangyayari at magaganap sa impeachment trial," Castro said.
(So even if most of them, or rather, some of them, join the majority, it does not mean they will dictate what will happen in the impeachment trial.)
Previously, during the Senate impeachment court's vote on lowering the threshold to convict Duterte in her trial, Villar was the lone senator from the minority who voted "yes."

With 13 "yes" votes from the senator-judges, the base for the two-thirds voting threshold was revised to only recognize senators who are capable of "legally and factually participating in the impeachment proceedings."
However, Castro called Villar's shift a "good message" as it could indicate that more senators now believe in the programs of the President, who aims to pass priority bills before his term ends.

"Mas maganda ang naging mensahe na ito dahil malamang mas marami na naniniwala sa kanila kung ano ba ang dapat na tunguhin at kung saan ba ang dapat na direksyon ng ating gobyerno pagdating sa pagpapagawa at pagsasabatas ng mga may kinalamang issue sa ating bansa," Castro said.

(This sends a better message because it likely shows that more of them believe in the direction and in the goals our government should pursue when it comes to crafting and enacting laws concerning key issues in our country.) — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Why SB19 joined Senate push to open global paths for Filipino creatives
articles.summary: P-pop icon SB19 leads local artists rallying behind a new Senate bill that aims to break down travel and visa barriers for Filipino creatives

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – When SB19 stepped into the Senate on September 30, it carried with them not just its recent global success at Lollapalooza. The five P-pop superstars also brought with them the stories and struggles most Filipino artists face when they travel and perform overseas.

SB19’s rise to stardom did not come without obstacles, so when the group visited the Senate to push for an act to promote global mobility of creative workers, it sparked appreciation from other artists who have been fighting for the same rights.

Introduced by Senator Bam Aquino, Senate Bill No. 2517 or the Philippine Agency for the Creative Economy (PACE) Act aims to strengthen the “international mobility of Filipino creative workers” and expand their “global opportunities and international market access for Philippine creative goods and services.”
The measure builds on Republic Act No. 11904, also known as the Philippine Creative Industries Development Act.

“We’re very happy that finally, it’s happening,” said SB19’s Stell. “Ever since we started as a group, we have many goals and visions that we want to achieve, not just for ourselves, but for the whole industry. We hope that [the Senate bill] flourishes and we hope to help.”
“It’s not just for ourselves….We want [other artists] to also experience relief, that they won’t experience the past problems we experienced,” he added in a mix of English and Filipino.

The bill offers assistance for international airfare and transportation, visa and travel documentation facilitation, travel insurance, and other financial or logistical assistance for an artist’s eligible international activities.
It covers not only singers and performers, but all Filipino creatives like filmmakers, animators, designers, game developers, writers, and cultural workers.

“We know how hard it is to perform in different cities, back-to-back shows. But you still have to think about your teams, you can’t bring them along because of visa problems, or the unapproved budgets for plane travels,” said Stell.
“It’s very hard for an artist….We’re artists, and at the same time, we’re wearing different hats. We’re also thinking about the problems of the team, our partners, and our overseas collaborators.”
It’s one reason SB19 got inspired to write the song “VISA” as the group members themselves experienced various issues when crossing borders with their creative teams.

“We’re very happy that the government is making a move and listening to us — our partners, the creators here in the Philippines in different forms, whether in film, beauty, fitness, athletes — the Philippines can really help and support them,” said Stell.
“That’s how we really are in the Philippines — we aim to support and help the people who bring pride and honor, not just here in the Philippines, but also outside the country.”
J2X, also known as “Coach Jay,” has been one of SB19’s choreographers since Day 1. But he also hopes to bring more of his own music beyond borders.
XONARA, a rising P-pop girl group under 1Z Entertainment — the talent management company founded by SB19 — hopes to benefit from the new industry measures as well.
“Gusto po naming mag-perform nang buong-buo para maranasan din po ng mga tao. Gusto po naming mag-perform po ulit sa stage and sobrang na-excite po talaga kami,” XONARA’s Lei said.
(We want to go all-out with our performance, and for people to experience it as well. We want to perform again onstage and we’re very excited.)
XONARA will also travel for the group’s first overseas show this October in Singapore.

“Actually, it is a huge privilege to perform internationally for a four-month-old group. It seems early, but we’re very thankful for those who believe in us that we can do it, and so we’re also trusting ourselves,” XONARA’s Eurekah said in Filipino.
“We’re hoping to represent Filipino talent in Singapore alongside other OPM artists, where together, we can share what Filipino talent really is.”
SB19 said it hopes the PACE Act can help artists still figuring their way around the industry, but reminded them that success still takes a lot of hard work.

“For the other artists who are dreaming to be here, in this kind of path, just listen to your heart. If this is what you really want, there’s no easy way,” said Stell. “You will really go through the hardships, and those hardships will teach you to be strong, to continue, and to remind you why you started.” – Rappler.com
Angel Camille Dio is a Rappler intern studying BA Journalism at Polytechnic University of the Philippines.

articles.title: Palantir’s Tom Watson says ‘mob rule’ must not dictate awarding of government contracts
articles.summary:
Former Labour deputy leader says tech firm would work with a Reform UK government on immigration crackdowns

Tom Watson, the former Labour deputy leader who recently joined Palantir, has…

blocks.text: Tom Watson, the former Labour deputy leader who recently joined Palantir, has warned against “mob rule” when it comes to awarding public contracts.

Lord Watson, now a senior vice-president at the US tech corporation, said UK ministers could get themselves “in a lot of trouble” as he was questioned about concerns raised about the government working with his new employer.

Palantir was co-founded by the Trump-supporting billionaire Peter Thiel and has provided AI-powered software to the Israeli military and the White House’s ICE immigration crackdown, leading to a public and political backlash against its deepening involvement in British public services.
The prime minister, Andy Burnham, is under significant pressure from Labour MPs and unions to ditch Palantir from government contracts, including a £330m software deal with the NHS.

The company is also fighting Sadiq Khan in court over the London mayor’s block on a £50m contract to use its AI in Metropolitan police investigations. It is also seeking to win more public sector work in the UK, where it already has an annual turnover of £427m.

Watson told the BBC podcast Political Thinking with Nick Robinson: “One of the things I’d say to my former colleagues is: do you want to let the rule of law lead procurement practice, or do you want to let mob rule to lead procurement practices? Because you get yourself in a lot of trouble if you go down on the latter one.”

He added: “I think we are very targeted by the people that are targeting Israeli companies. We’re not an Israeli company, but because of our work in Israel, we found ourselves in the middle of the row of the Gaza protests.”
Watson told the podcast he would work with a Reform UK government on immigration crackdowns if the situation arose, saying: “We don’t actually work in that sector, but yes, of course we would.”

He called Palantir “the most interesting company on the planet” as he announced his new role last month. His job would be, in part, to “deepen the social and economic value its work creates through better British public services, jobs and skills”, Palantir said.

Watson was a defence minister and a minister for digital engagement in Gordon Brown’s government. Since stepping down from parliament in 2019, he has been an adviser to the gambling and music industries and, since 2024, he has been a part-time adviser to Palantir.
after newsletter promotion
Palantir said Watson had taken a leave of absence from the House of Lords and had relinquished his parliamentary pass while he works for the company in London.

The Labour MP Chi Onwurah, who chairs the science, innovation and technology committee, which has raised concerns about Palantir, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: “Tom is not the first politician to be blinded by tech hype. The key issue is we can’t be so dependent on one company. It’s a US company, subject to US legislation regarding access to our data.”

articles.title: Labour fends off Green party to win Holborn and St Pancras byelection
articles.summary: Victory by Sagal Abdi-Wali in north London seat will be a relief for Andy Burnham in high-stakes battle for the left of British politics

blocks.text: Labour has seen off the Greens to win the Holborn and St Pancras byelection in a result that will relieve Andy Burnham and dent Zack Polanski’s position as a decisive power player on the left of British politics.

The byelection, called after former prime minister Keir Starmer resigned from the seat in September, was considered a two-horse race between the Labour candidate, Sagal Abdi-Wali, and the Green party leader, Polanski. Abdi-Wali received 12,292 votes, 45% of the vote, to Polanski’s 8,928, 33% of the vote.
Turnout was 38.7%, the lowest for any byelection held in England during this parliament and 15.4% down from the 2024 general election.

In an emotional victory speech, Abdi-Wali, a former child refugee who came to the UK from Somalia in the 1990s, hit out at “those who seek to divide us” in what appeared to be a response to Reform UK’s Zia Yusuf, who suggested she was not British shortly after the byelection was called.

“I hope this moment says something about who gets to belong,” she said. “For people who look like me. I hope they see themselves reflected in this place and know that their path too belongs here. This is Camden and this is Britain.”

Labour’s victory provides assurance for Burnham in his first big electoral test as prime minister, and reinforces polling that shows he has recovered some public support lost by Starmer, his predecessor in Downing Street.
However, the low turnout suggests Burnham still faces an uphill battle in urban areas, particularly in the capital where the Greens took control of three councils in May’s local elections.

blocks.caption: Zack Polanski, Green Party leader, at the Holborn and St Pancras byelection count. Photograph: James Veysey/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Polanski’s loss caps a bruising week for his eco-populist party, which fell into turmoil after it voted on Sunday to adopt a policy declaring Zionism a form of racism, raising questions about his leadership.

Shortly after polls closed, Caroline Lucas refused to say whether Polanski should stand down. Speaking to BBC Newsnight, the former Green party leader said: “I want him to show the leadership that was frankly missing on Sunday,” when the motion was voted on. Polanski abstained and campaigned in the constituency instead.

Speaking to the BBC after the result came in, Polanski insisted he would remain in his post. “Of course I can carry on as leader of the Green party,” he said. “We’re a party of 220,000 members. I’ve taken a loss tonight but our movement is so much bigger than one election or one motion and we’re going to grow.”

The motion at the centre of the fallout said Zionism – the movement for a Jewish state – should be “treated as any other form of racism” and called for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state. The head of the Jewish Greens condemned the motion and said she might leave the party, although it was supported by some Jewish Greens.

The motion passed in a vote by Green members at the party conference despite opposition from four of its five MPs. Even members who supported large parts of the motion were unhappy about its narrow conception of Zionism, which some fear could brand those in favour of the idea of a Jewish homeland, but not specifically the modern-day state of Israel, as racist.

Asked after the result whether he believed Zionism was racism, Polanski said he “grew up in a Zionist household” with the “idea that region was a land without a people and a people without a land”. But he said after educating himself he doesn’t “believe that’s true, and what we’re seeing is an ongoing genocide and the displacement of the Palestinian people. I believe that’s clearly racist.”

blocks.caption: Candidates on stage as the declaration is made in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection. Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PA

blocks.text: Speaking to the Guardian after her win, Abdi-Wali said local people at the school gates found the Greens motion “divisive”, adding: “It just speaks to the larger divisive discourse that set off and I don’t want to engage in that kind of thing.”

On Labour’s stance on Palestine, she said: “The work Ed Miliband has been doing on Gaza, Palestine and Israel has resonated really well with local people. He’s been taking action and not just speaking.”

The Greens’ standing in the polls, and Polanski’s personal approval ratings, had fallen in recent months after a peak in popularity last summer, exemplified by the party’s seismic win in the Gorton and Denton byelection in February.

The Greens ran a strong ground game, dispatching thousands of members to knock on doors in the constituency, even before Polanski was selected as the party’s candidate. But the 8,928 votes cast for Polanski compares to the nearly 11,350 his party and Andrew Feinstein – a pro-Gaza figure on the left – received combined in the seat in 2024 suggests the Greens have not significantly expanded their base of voters in the constituency.

On the contest’s low turnout, Liam Conlon, Labour MP for Beckenham and Penge and the campaign leader for Abdi-Wali told the Guardian: “We performed better tonight than we did in May at the local elections here. That shows you the direction of travel.”

Midway into the race, George Galloway, running in “self-exile” outside the UK, put his name on the ballot in a move that many Green supporters said could pull votes away from Polanski. In the end, he received 314 votes.

articles.title: Albay mayors give ALECO ultimatum to solve persistent power interruptions
articles.summary: The electric cooperative attributes the outages to ongoing national-funded substation upgrades, promising Phase 1 completion in 2026 amid rising public frustration over their unreliable services

blocks.text: BRIEFING. ALECO head of operations Mark Lucilo (extreme right) explains the reasons behind the persistent power outages that have disrupted various towns in recent months in 2026.
Caloy Baldo/Facebook page
The electric cooperative attributes the outages to ongoing national-funded substation upgrades, promising Phase 1 completion in 2026 amid rising public frustration over their unreliable services

items: Mayors in Albay are demanding an end to weekly power interruptions and have threatened to report ALECO if improvements are not seen by the end of October.

ALECO attributes the ongoing power cuts to necessary infrastructure upgrades and has received significant government funding for these projects, but consumers continue to face high electricity bills and unreliable service.
Albay Governor Noel Rosal has called for a comprehensive plan from ALECO to address the power issues, emphasizing the need for transparency and accountability in their operations.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

ALBAY, Philippines – Mayors in Albay demanded an immediate end to weekly power interruptions across various towns during the League of Municipalities of the Philippines (LMP) Albay Chapter meeting with the Albay Electric Cooperative (ALECO) on Wednesday, October 7.

“The stand of the mayors was clear — after this month, if the power service does not improve or change, we will immediately report ALECO again,” Camalig town Mayor and LMP-Albay President Caloy Baldo said in Bicol.
According to Baldo, ALECO promised the LMP-Albay Chapter that the series of power interruptions would ease and eventually be resolved by the end of October 2026.
“In the next meeting, we encourage the general nanager and ALECO’s contractor to appear in person so they can directly answer the mayors’ remaining questions,” he added.
ALECO explained that the ongoing interruptions were inevitable due to system improvements, maintenance, upgrades, and rehabilitation projects across the cooperative’s network.

According to the cooperative, recent power cuts were caused by the installation of a 1×20 MegaVolt-Amperes (MVA) transformer at the Cullat substation and the upgrading of the Ligao Substation in Dunao, Ligao City from 20MVA to 40MVA.

“These infrastructure improvements involve construction, installation, rehabilitation, and upgrading of electrical facilities that require the temporary de-energization of portions of the distribution system to ensure the safety of personnel and the public while the necessary works are being undertaken,” ALECO said in its statement posted on Thursday, October 8.
The cooperative emphasized that these upgrades are necessary to enhance system reliability, improve voltage regulation, and support the growing power demand across Albay’s municipalities.

“These projects should be finished by the end of October, but sometimes factors arise that cause extensions. However, we are 100% sure that phase 1 construction of the substation, which costs P367 million, will be completed within 2026,” ALECO head of operations Mark Lucilo explained in Bicol.
In 2025, the cooperative received a P367-million national government funding for the upgrade and rehabilitation of distribution lines and substations across several towns in the province.

On top of this rehabilitation fund, ALECO was awarded an additional P500-million subsidy from the National Electrification Administration (NEA) under the General Appropriations Act, through the initiative of the Ako Bicol (AKB) Party-list, to construct new substations in Ligao City and Daraga town.

ALECO board of directors president Eddie Gumba told DZGB News Online, a local radio station in Albay, that these substations aim to deliver reliable and stable power service while minimizing the frequent power interruptions across Albay.

Despite over P867 million in combined government grants and subsidies since 2025, consumers continue to bear the brunt of both frequent blackouts and skyrocketing electricity rates, according to Legazpi City resident Jeric Azores.

“Our bill nearly doubled despite persistent power interruptions. It’s deeply frustrating because, on top of disrupting our daily household routines and business transactions, we are paying significantly more for electricity while Albay’s power services remain completely unreliable,” Azores said.
Earlier in July 2026, Albay Governor Noel Rosal demanded that ALECO submit a comprehensive plan to address recurring power interruptions and inadequate electricity supply in the province.

“We need a report from the board so that both the administration and the consumers can decide how we can help resolve this and determine whether we should continue relying on ALECO,” Rosal said. “If we see that their plan is doable, why look for another distributor? But they must prove their plans and explain them to the public — especially regarding debt servicing, given their existing debt of around P5 billion to P6 billion.”

The governor added that ALECO’s operational and financial report must be presented during a Special Annual General Membership Assembly to ensure transparency, accountability, and active stakeholder participation.
Meanwhile, the LMP-Albay Chapter also reminded ALECO to keep communication lines open to address consumer concerns promptly, especially during unscheduled power interruptions.

“Mayors hope for a final solution to the electricity problem so government agencies can deliver better, more efficient service, ensuring Albayanos receive the quality service they deserve,” Baldo said.

He added: “We will continue to support the cooperative and extend help to ALECO, but we also need to stand firm for a more reliable, faster, and better electricity service for our fellow citizens.” –Rappler.com

articles.title: Please, sir, can I have a walk? Dickens biographer finds likely inspiration for Oliver Twist
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Theresa Musgrove unearths newspaper archives showing one Alice Shepherd was severely punished in 1836 for similarly innocent request

Could a consumptive young woman called Alice…

blocks.text: Could a consumptive young woman called Alice Shepherd have been the inspiration for Oliver Twist? That is a question now being posed by a historian, who has discovered parallels between the brutality suffered by a real-life pauper incarcerated in one of Victorian London’s notorious workhouses and Charles Dickens’s fictional orphan.

In researching a new book on Dickens, Theresa Musgrove unearthed 1836 newspaper reports on Alice Shepherd, who endured starvation and solitary confinement within a workhouse in Hendon, after a magistrate ruled she was to be punished for daring to ask for permission to take a walk.

In his classic novel, which was published in monthly instalments from 1837 to 1839, Dickens wrote that nine-year-old Oliver was hauled up before a magistrate and imprisoned in a “dark and solitary room” for having the temerity to ask for a second helping of gruel, with the poignant words: “Please, sir, I want some more.”
The starving child was locked up for week. Dickens wrote: “Oliver was the victim of a systematic course of treachery and deception.”

blocks.caption: An illustration by James Mahoney from The Adventures of Oliver Twist, Chapman and Hall edition, 1838. Original caption: ‘Stop thief; Oliver is pursued by an angry crowd.’ Photograph: Bridgeman/Getty Images

blocks.text: Newspaper reports record that Alice Shepherd was put in a “straightjacket”, having been “in a state of great agitation”. A Rev Theodore Williams, in his capacity as a magistrate and chair of the local board of guardians responsible for overseeing the conduct of Hendon’s old workhouse, recommended a punishment for her “disgusting conduct”.
She was put in solitary confinement for 24 hours, and starved on a diet of bread and water until the next meeting of the board – which met once a fortnight.

Another local magistrate, also one of the workhouse’s guardians of the board, tried in vain to defend her, arguing that such “a thin spare woman apparently suffering from consumption … [was the] last person … to whom such a punishment should have been inflicted”.
Musgrove told the Guardian: “When you read the report of her punishment, it is almost, word for word, like a description of Oliver Twist when he is punished after asking for more.”

She said: “The reaction to Oliver Twist’s ‘impertinence’ in asking for more food is perhaps an echo of Alice’s daring to ask to go out for a walk: a reasonable request met by fury by those whose job it was to enforce the unremitting authority of the board of guardians, by whose mercy the undeserving poor were granted the means of a life of such bleak subsistence.”
Her research features in her new book, titled Charles Dickens and his Hidden Family History, which is published this week by Pen & Sword Books.

She writes: “Both Oliver and Alice were subjected to solitary confinement, and yet, as we learn, the parish boy’s punishment was to be considered not so bad because he was allowed out into the stone yard to wash under the pump, just as Reverend Williams pointed out … that the room appropriated for the solitary confinement and starvation of Alice Shepherd ‘looked upon the yard where all the other paupers were, and therefore, was not a very severe punishment’.

“In mid-January, within weeks of this story being reported, Dickens was writing to his publisher Bentley that he had ‘hit upon a capital notion for myself, and one which will bring Cruikshank out’. In other words, the creation of Oliver Twist had begun, and indeed the first chapters would be published in February 1837, illustrated by the starkly graphic work of George Cruikshank.”
after newsletter promotion

She notes that Dickens was familiar with Hendon, in the present-day London borough of Barnet: “Hendon and Barnet are mentioned, for example, in Oliver Twist … but also there are other references in his letters and journalism that reveal a knowledge of Hendon and a fondness for the area, which was within walking or riding distance of the city itself, a quiet landscape of villages and farmland.

“In the later stages of Oliver Twist, after his brutal killing of Nancy, Bill Sikes goes on the run … After sleeping rough, Sikes heads off towards Hendon, but the people there seem suspicious of him and he goes back to the Heath.”

Oliver Twist exposed the brutality of poverty in Victorian Britain. Dickens became a tireless campaigner for social reform, having been scarred by his own childhood experiences after his father was incarcerated in a debtors’ prison and, aged about 12, he was sent to work in a blacking factory.

Leon Litvack, a leading Dickens expert and professor of Victorian studies at Queen’s University Belfast, said it was “perfectly feasible” that Dickens was inspired by Alice Shepherd, as newspaper reports were among “an amalgam of influences that sparked his imagination, distilled into a coherent narrative”, particularly early in his career.

He added: “Dickens was a journalist before he was a novelist, so he was well aware of the power of sensation. He was fascinated by the workhouse and aware of what was appearing in the press about particular abuses.”

articles.title: ICC says experts found Duterte's health improved while in detention
articles.summary: The International Criminal Court"s expert panel that checked on former President Rodrigo Duterte to determine his fitness to stand trial saw “an apparent improvement” in his health while detained.

blocks.text: Published October 9, 2026 2:54pm
The International Criminal Court’s expert panel that checked on former President Rodrigo Duterte to determine his fitness to stand trial saw “an apparent improvement” in his health while detained.
Duterte is on trial for crimes against humanity related to the deaths attributed to his war on drugs when he was President and when he was mayor of Davao City.

“With respect to the Accused’s general health condition, the Expert Panel reports that his ‘general physical health appears to have been optimized,” the court said in its decision to declare Duterte fit to stand trial.

“Expert Panel observes that there is an ‘apparent improvement in Mr Duterte’s health since [its] previous report’ and explains that such an improvement is attributable to ‘the high standard of medical and nursing care, including diagnostic rigor and pharmacological rationalization’,” it added.
The court said the expert panel acknowledges that Duterte:

items: has some physical and mental slowing in keeping with his age; and
may be subject to fatigue (tiring) in keeping with his age and frailty.

blocks.text: “The members of the Expert Panel further note that ‘[i]t is not possible to rule out that he may have some mild or pre-clinical process of slowing… and that, ‘[w]hile other mental capacities such as memory may be reduced compared to when he was younger, we can find no reliable evidence of this on formal testing’,” the court said.

“Nonetheless, the Chamber observes that the members of the expert panel are unanimous in their finding that ‘any reduced mental capacity present is not such as to render Mr Duterte unable to fulfill the necessary capacities,” it added.

The International Criminal Court Trial Chamber III has found former President Rodrigo Duterte fit to stand trial, stating that he “is able to effectively exercise his fair trial rights in the proceedings.”

The Trial Chamber III made public on Thursday, October 8, a decision dated September 28, which stated it was “satisfied that the Expert Panel’s Reports are sufficiently conclusive to decide on the Accused’ ability to participate in the trial proceedings and to effectively exercise his procedural and fair trial rights.”
Trial Chamber III also ordered measures to facilitate Duterte’s participation in the proceedings. The trial is scheduled to open on Nov. 30, 2026.
The Chamber’s decision came as it found that Duterte’s defense “misrepresents the instructions the Chamber gave to the Expert Panel.” –NB, GMA News
